```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_sf <- requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)
```

Nonparametric tests of spatial independence on neighbourhood graphs. Companion software to E. Ashtari Nezhad, *A nonparametric test of spatial independence on neighbourhood graphs*. A Python version with
the same functions and output is on PyPI (`pip install ivspatial`).

## 1. What the package does

`ivspatial` tests whether the values of a variable observed at spatial units
(cells of a grid, polygons such as counties, irregularly located points, or the
nodes of a network) are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.)
across the units. The tests are **rank based and exact**: under independence
the P-value is valid for every sample size, every graph and every continuous
distribution, with no weight matrix, bandwidth or model to choose. The package
reports

* the P-value of the proposed **combined test C4** and of its four
  components: **T_V(4,3)**, which sees dependence among a site and two of its
  neighbours, including dependence that is invisible in every pair;
  **T_V(4,2)**, pairs with finely resolved tails; **RM**, the Moran statistic of
  the ranks (level); and **RS**, the Moran statistic of the squared ranks
  (scale);
* asymptotic P-values from the explicit weighted chi-square limits;
* seven **standardized features**, which tell whether the dependence is in the
  level, in the scale or between neighbours;
* **maps** of local feature contributions, which show where the dependence
  occurs;
* a **data-driven choice of the resolution**, statistics at **several spatial
  lags**, **screening** of many variables with false discovery rate control,
  and tests for **regression residuals**.

## 2. Two ways to use it

* **The window (no programming).** `ivspatial_app()` opens the graphical
  interface in the browser: open a table or a polygon file (or an example),
  build the neighbourhood graph, pick a variable and press *Run test*. Maps,
  the null distribution and this guide are in their own tabs.
* **R code**, shown below. Both give the same results.

## 3. The neighbourhood graph

The neighbourhood of a site is the site and its neighbours; the graph says
which sites are considered close.

| Data | Function | Typical choice |
|---|---|---|
| points | `knn_graph(xy, k)` | k = 4 to 6 |
| points | `delaunay_graph(xy)` (package deldir) | contiguity of Voronoi cells |
| points | `distance_band_graph(xy, radius)` | check that few sites are isolated |
| grid | `lattice_graph(nrow, ncol)`, `lattice_from_indices(row, col)` | rook (4 neighbours) |
| polygons | `polygon_graph(x, "queen")` (package sf) | queen |
| network | `graph_from_edges(i, j)`, `graph_from_neighbors(nb)` | the links |

```{r}
library(ivspatial)
g <- lattice_from_indices(mercer_hall$row, mercer_hall$col, "rook")
g
```

## 4. Testing one variable

```{r}
res <- spatial_test(mercer_hall$grain, g, B = 999, seed = 1, label = "grain")
res
```

* **C4** is the proposed test: a P-value below the level means that the values
  are not i.i.d. across the sites. The smallest possible P-value is
  1/(B + 1); use B = 9999 (the default) for reporting.
* The **components** show which aspect carries the evidence. The
  **asymptotic** P-values use the weighted chi-square limit and agree with the
  exact ones in large samples.
* The **standardized features** are approximately standard normal under
  independence. Here `c.lin|n.lin` and `n.lin^2` are large: plots resemble
  their neighbours in level, while the scale features are small.

The elements of the result can be used directly:

```{r}
res$p_value
res$components[, c("name", "statistic", "p_value")]
as.data.frame(res)[, 1:5]
```

## 5. Points, residuals and many variables

```{r}
gk <- knn_graph(cbind(baltimore$X, baltimore$Y), k = 4)
spatial_test(log(baltimore$PRICE), gk, B = 999, seed = 1, features = FALSE)
```

Residuals of a regression with exogenous regressors are tested without any
correction (not for spatial-lag models, in which y is regressed on its own
spatial lag):

```{r}
r <- residual_test(log(baltimore$PRICE), baltimore[, c("NROOM", "NBATH", "SQFT", "AGE")], gk,
                   B = 999, seed = 1)
r$p_value
r$features
```

Several variables on the same graph share one table of random rank
arrangements, and the P-values are adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg method:

```{r}
screen_variables(mercer_hall, g, columns = c("grain", "straw"), B = 999, seed = 1)
```

## 6. Polygons

```{r, eval = has_sf}
nc <- read_polygons(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"))
gq <- polygon_graph(nc, "queen")
gq
spatial_test(1000 * nc$SID79 / nc$BIR79, gq, B = 999, seed = 1, features = FALSE)
```

## 7. Maps of local features

Every feature is a scaled sum of local contributions, one per site, each with
mean 0 and variance 1 under independence. Mapping them shows where a feature
receives its contribution, as local indicators of spatial association do for
Moran's I. The maps are descriptive, not tests.

```{r, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 3.4}
map_local(mercer_hall$grain, lattice_graph(20, 25))
```

`local_features(x, g)` returns the contributions as a data frame.

## 8. Data-driven resolution and spatial lags

With `resolution = "auto"` the data choose among T_V(d, s), d = 2 to 6,
s = 2, 3, by the minimum-P rule; the selection is repeated in every random
rank arrangement, so the P-value is exact after selection. `"schwarz"` uses a
penalized choice that prefers simple statistics. With `lags = 2` the
components are also computed for the neighbours at graph distance two.

```{r}
a <- spatial_test(mercer_hall$straw, g, B = 499, seed = 1, resolution = "auto", features = FALSE,
                  asymptotic = FALSE)
a$selected
a$p_value
```

## 9. The null limit

Under independence T_V(d, s) converges to a weighted sum of chi-square
variables with one degree of freedom; the weights are the eigenvalues of the
exact covariance matrix of the features on the graph.

```{r}
null_limit(g, d = 4, s = 2, value = 35)
```

## 10. Notes

* The null hypothesis is that the values are i.i.d. A smooth trend or
  heteroskedasticity is detected as dependence; model the trend and test the
  residuals if needed.
* Missing values are not allowed: remove the incomplete sites and build the
  graph for the remaining ones.
* Ties (discrete data) are broken at random, which keeps the tests exact.
* The user guide with screenshots of the window: `ivspatial_guide()`.

## Reference

Ashtari Nezhad, E. (2026). A nonparametric test of spatial independence on neighbourhood graphs. Manuscript.
